idiom_name: no inheritance: consumer-defined interface or func-field seam
implementation_notes: Go deliberately has no type inheritance - methods are bound to a named type and embedding promotes methods without ever overriding their dispatch, so the classic 'subclass the SUT and override the self-call' move is unavailable; the FAQ's answer is interfaces and composition. The idiomatic seam is a small interface declared by the consumer (or a func field on the struct) whose production implementation is swapped for a fake in the test; keep the interface next to its user so it stays narrow, and prefer a simple hand-written fake struct over generated mocks.
pitfalls: Embedding a concrete type does not create an override: struct{ RealClock } keeps dispatching to RealClock's methods - there is no virtual call to intercept.
A func-field seam needs an explicit nil check or a default, and a nil interface panics rather than falling back to production behaviour.
Declaring the interface in the production package instead of at the consumption point couples the fake to a wide, producer-shaped API and re-creates the dependency the seam was meant to remove.
alternative: Extract the boundary behind a small consumer-defined interface (or a func field) and inject a stub/fake - Dependency Injection - because Go has no subclassing and embedding does not override method dispatch.
